subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF THIRTY-SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF D-DAY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under Standing Order 43 concerning a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
On Sunday, June 6, 1976, Canadian veterans of World War II will remember the D-Day invasion of Normandy by allied forces. Unfortunately, thousands of our Canadian youth lie in graves in France because of this holocaust and it is our duty that parliament pay respect for those who fell. I therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton):
That this House gives recognition and pays tribute to war veterans who took part and to the families of those who fell on June 6, 1944 on this, the 32nd anniversary of D-Day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Having regard to the huge supply of skim milk powder in storage in Eastern Canada, estimated at well in excess of 200 million pounds, and the fact that export sales remain at prices below 10 cents per pound as animal feed while domestic prices are being held in the 40-50 cent range, and given the fact that domestic markets are available in the West for feed grade skimmed milk powder at reasonable prices for use as milk replacer, calf starter and poultry rations, but that insufficient stocks exist there to meet the demand, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
That the Minister of Agriculture instruct the Canadian Dairy Commission to release sufficient quantities of skim milk powder at reasonable prices to the animal feed industry to fulfil present and future demands, so as to improve the viability of this important industry and at the same time reduce feed costs to these animal producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the authorization for payment of the interest was decided by Treasury Board after December 2. The memorandum dated December 1, prepared
Oral Questions
by my officials, pertaining to the LRPA project, referred to possible cash flow problems with regard to the most cost-effective production schedule. The memorandum indicated that to respect the most efficient schedule DND could possibly resort to commercial financing. No reference was made to financial negotiations held between Lockheed and DND. A copy of this memorandum was sent to the official of DND responsible for the LRPA program. Later that day this same DND official, as well as my own officials, met with me for a briefing session in preparation for a meeting to be held with Lockheed representatives the following day. In both instances, during the briefing session of December 1 and during the December 2 meeting with Lockheed representatives, Mr. Kotchian and his associates, the Department of National Defence, which in this case had exclusive responsibility to provide financing, made no reference to financial negotiations held between Lockheed and itself. Furthermore, DND gave no indication whatsoever that it could not meet its financial obligations. At that point in time I had no apparent reason to mistrust the DND's judgment.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the contented Minister of Finance concerning certain budgetary proposals he made a year ago. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration in committee described as a red herring those who wanted to change the UIC Act away from providing for claimants who have spent eight weeks in the labour force by saying that this would particularly affect the people in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Specifically the minister said:
The incidence of disentitlement or disqualification, as an effect of failure to meet one's obligation under the act, is lower amongst the group with a minor attachment to the work force-
I should like to ask the minister if that was the government's view last year and, since my information is that the evidence has not changed one whit, why has the government changed its policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REASON FOR CHANGES IN UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, in his statement the other day, pointed out that the careful analysis which the government has had from the Unemployment Insurance Commission about the profile of this particular group in the work force is one which has just been available to the government in recent months and which of course has been reinforced by the careful analysis the government and the country has received from the Economic Council with regard to jobs and the work force and the best way to deal with one of the priority problems in Canada.

I should like to ask this as a supplementary: since the Minister of Manpower and Immigration also said last year that the particular nature of the labour market in Atlantic Canada made it essential to maintain the Act as it was and said most specifically:
... I think we get at the root of upgrading their opportunity rather than trying to cut them off because they are a cost or an embarrassment. They would be on welfare anyway ...
It was his view that welfare costs were bound to increase for the Atlantic provinces if the Act were changed in this direction. I should like to ask the minister what evidence he has for believing today that welfare costs will not substantially increase in Atlantic Canada as a result of this change.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I stated in the House on May 18 that information concerning the position which Canada will take at the forthcoming ICNAF meeting would be conveyed to the House. Our position at the ICNAF meeting cannot be discussed separately from our position on extended Canadian fisheries' jurisdiction to 200 miles. I wish to make a statement on both these issues and to announce today the government's decision to extend the fisheries jurisdiction of Canada out to 200 miles from the coast.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext:
Implementation of this decision under existing Canadian legislation will come later this year, and in any event will be in place by January 1, 1977. The state of our fishery resource and the situation of our fishermen, of our fishing industry, and of our coastal communities, make this action imperative. There will be no fishery resource left to protect if action is not taken now, because the fish stocks will be so depleted as to disappear as a resource of commercial significance. Not only the fish, but our Canadian fishermen too are an "endangered species", as I have heard them describe themselves.
The protection of Canadian interests is of concern to us as a result of the extension of U.S. fisheries jurisdiction in March, 1977. Mexico, our other neighbour on the North American continent, has left compelled to act and has recently adopted legislation to bring about an extension of jurisdiction to 200 miles.

The government last year instructed Canadian officials to conduct bilateral negotiations with major fishing states operating off the Canadian coast regarding the terms and conditions that Canada will apply when permitting foreign fisheries in respect of any resources surplus to Canadian harvesting capacity within Canada's 200-mile zone. Agreements have been signed with Norway, Poland and the U.S.S.R., as well as ad referendum agreements with Spain and Portugal, in addition to the agreement with France entered into in 1972. These various agreements, when they are all in place, will cover major foreign fisheries off Canada's Pacific coast and more than 88 per cent of the foreign catch in that part of the ICNAF convention area to be incorporated within Canada's 200-mile zone. They will provide for a smooth transition to the new regime of extended Canadian fisheries jurisdiction.
There will be a continuing need, following extensions of fisheries jurisdiction by coastal states, for multilateral fisheries co-operation. New multilateral arrangements will be needed to bring the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries-ICNAF-and other fisheries conventions into line with the new jurisdictional realities. The instructions to the Canadian delegation to the ICNAF meeting in June have been formulated on the basis of Canada's decision to extend its fisheries jurisdiction by January 1, 1977. The delegation has been instructed to make clearly known to other delegations Canada's intention regarding extension of jurisdiction and possible future multilateral arrangements for the northwest Atlantic.
We will also give notice to other nations fishing off our coast that conservation and management measures for 1977 will be established by Canada to provide for effective protection and rebuilding of the stocks and must ensure, within such conservation limits, that the needs of Canadian fishermen are satisfied. At the same time, we are prepared to commit ourselves, as we already have in the bilateral agreements, to allow other nations to fish in Canada's 200-mile zone for stocks surplus to Canada's harvesting capacity, and to carry out appropriate consultations with such countries in the development of regulations within the zone. We are prepared to co-operate with other nations in this way, but in return we expect their co-operation in achieving our objectives.
I wish to emphasize that the government will in no way abandon its deep commitment to reaching multilateral solutions to problems of the Law of the Sea in general, and fisheries in particular. We will continue to work within the UN conference on the Law of the Sea to reach agreement not only on fisheries but also on the other vital and difficult issues facing the conference, issues such as the establishment of an international authority for the management of the resources of the deep seabed and ocean floor which constitute the "common heritage of mankind"; the preservation and protection of the marine environment, including the Arctic; and the breadth of the territorial sea and the other related question of passage through straits used for international navigation. These issues must find an early multilateral solution.
We knew from the outset that the spring session of the Law of the Sea conference in New York could not achieve final agreement on a new convention. At least one more session will be necessary for this purpose, and the confer-
June 4, 1976

ence will convene again in New York from August 2 to September 17. We hope it will succeed, but must anticipate that even then there would still be formalities to be concluded. I said at the United Nations General Assembly last fall, then at the Law of the Sea conference in New York, and most recently in the House of Commons, that 1976 must be the year of decision for the conference. I wish to make clear here and now that 1976 is also the year of decision for Canada's extension of fisheries jurisdiction out to 200 miles.
The decision I am announcing today to extend Canada's fisheries jurisdiction does not constitute unilateral action that either leaves no room for negotiation or ignores the interests of other countries directly concerned. It is action for which we have carefully prepared the way through both bilateral and regional negotiations within ICNAF and within the multilateral framework of the Law of the Sea conference. It is action based on a growing consensus among nations, a consensus which is increasingly finding its way into state practice and is reflected in the provisions of the single negotiating text that emerged from last year's session of the Law of the Sea conference in Geneva and has been confirmed in this year's revised text. It is action that is based on Canada's obligation as a good steward or custodian to protect and preserve a perishable resource which is increasingly threatened with depletion while growing in importance as a source of food for the world at large. It is action that will ensure the fishery resources off the Canadian coast can be managed wisely for the benefit of Canadians and, indeed, of the entire world.
In conclusion, Canada is better prepared than perhaps any other country for extension of fisheries jurisdiction. Since the amendment of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone Act in 1970, we already have the necessary enabling legislation for establishment of the 200-mile limit and, after giving statutory notice, need only promulgate an order in council. That order in council will be promulgated at an appropriate time this year so as to have the 200-mile limit in place for January 1, 1977. We have also completed the necessary technical preparation. We have already concluded much of the necessary negotiation with the major distant-water fishing states concerned. Above all, we have the expertise and determination to carry through and implement our extended jurisdiction in an effective way, without rancour, without confrontation and without prejudicing the hope we share with the world that a multilateral solution to fisheries problems can ultimately be found, even while states take the national measures of protection that are so urgently needed.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the minister and would like to congratulate him for finally making this most welcome announcement concerning Canada's extention of its limit to 200 miles. The Progressive Conservative party has long advocated a 200-mile limit, and it is good to see the government finally following suit. I should like at this time, also, to thank the minister for the courtesy he has extended the official opposition by making a copy of his statement available prior to its presentation in the House, a practice that I would suggest might well be followed by other ministers of the Crown in making important national statements.
Fisheries
The minister has rightfully pointed out that "the state of our fishing resource and the situation of our fishermen, of our fishing industry, and of our coastal communities make this action imperative". There will be no fishery resource left to protect if action is not taken now, because the fish stocks will be so depleted as to disappear as a resource of commercial significance. There is nothing I could do to condemn more adequately the inaction of the government in this important matter to date than by referring to a similar statement by a previous Liberal minister, as follows:
Now we are engaged in an even bigger enterprise; one which will have the support of at least two-thirds of the membership of the UN; one which will almost certainly carry the day at the next Law of the Sea conference; one which will bring practically all of our offshore fish stocks under Canadian control.
This was a statement by Jack Davis on May 23, over three full years ago. Naturally, our party and the Canadian people wonder what caused this delay, for because of this delay the Canadian fishermen, the Canadian fishing industry and the Canadian economy as a whole have suffered heavily. Now, the fishermen-certainly those in Atlantic Canada-are adopting a "wait and see" attitude. "We will believe it when we see it", seems to be their view, and this is understandable. In 1972, for example, total fish landings in Canada were 2,258 million pounds; in 1973, they were 2,190 million pounds, in 1974, 1,839 million pounds; and in 1975, 1,578 million pounds-or a full 30 per cent decrease from 1972 figures. For particular species such as redfish, the situation is even worse. The redfish fishery is near a state of collapse, producing a situation pitting Canadian against Canadian, because certain areas of the Gulf have been closed to certain Nova Scotia and Newfoundland fishing vessels. As a result, we have had to go begging to the Russians for part of their redfish quota. This would not have happened if we had declared a 200-mile limit earlier.
The minister also has said that the bilateral agreements will provide for a smooth transition to the new regime of extended Canadian fisheries jurisdiction. But do they really? I have pointed out previously in this House that the wording of the recent Canada-U.S.S.R. fishing agreement is not clear as to what extent Russia would recognize or even obey a Canadian directive, especially if it was directed to fish for less quota. The Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) recently signed an agreement in Moscow which gave to the Russians an increased quota in caplin in exchange for some of the redfish quota which they presently have. But I would remind the House that the redfish quota given up by the Russians was not on the Soviet shelf but was on our own shelf. I would also remind the House of a fact which seems to be ingored by the present government, namely, that there is some order in the food chain and that the caplin quotas should have been reduced rather than increased because caplin is the food stock for all our groundfish species. If our groundfish stocks are to be rebuilt, we must make those original food stocks available in the food chain.
This raises another matter. The Department of Fisheries officials, ICNAF officials and the Fisheries Council of Canada-in fact, almost everyone but the Minister of State for Fisheries-have asserted that Canadian fishing

June 4, 1976
Fisheries
research is less than adequate. We do not know the breeding patterns of most fish species, nor how much fish there is within the 200-mile limit, nor how much fish should be caught. Presently, we rely to a great extent on the fisheries research of other nations. The Fisheries Council of Canada has decried this fact. The fishing industry on the east coast has offered to take scientists, free of charge, out on their boats to conduct research and, on the west coast, the Pacific Trawlers Association has offered additional funding to the department for its research program. Both offers were refused. What sort of attitude is this?
By his actions, the minister has allocated quotas and allowable fish catches without knowing the quantity of the stocks available. I say that one of the most important steps now required is an increase in fisheries research. We must formulate discussions with the industry on our long-range fisheries goals and plans for management of all marine stocks off our coasts. We need an increase in personnel, equipment and facilities in order to do this work, and wherever possible this work could, and should, be done from Canadian commercial fishing ships. Only in this way can we be assured that the stocks will be rebuilt. Unless this happens, the 200-mile limit declaration, which should offer a challenge, only becomes an illusion. The announcement is welcome, but it is only a beginnings-just one small step. There is much more to be done before the Canadian fishery can recover and regain its former good health.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we too, in the New Democratic Party welcome the announcement today. It is better late than not at all. I should like to say that in spite of the myriad problems facing our fishermen on both coasts, the announcement of a 200-mile limit

which has long been advocated by the fishermen of the west coast-will go some distance toward assisting us in the protection of our stocks. However, I cannot unreservedly be congratulatory with respect to the 200-mile zone from the point of view of the Pacific coast. First of all, we have some very serious problems on the Panhandle in negotiating catches with the United States. We have some very serious problems in terms of interception of salmon on the coast. These problems need more active attention by this government. They must be resolved, and until they are the 200-mile declaration can be quite empty and useless.
The position Canada has taken at the Law of the Sea conference for a long time has been a 200-mile zone or the continental margin. On the east coast, only a Liberal fishing policy, it seems to me, could have put the "Greenpeace" organization in the same camp as the Fishermen's Union of Newfoundland. Amazingly enough, they are now both together in opposition to the kind of Liberal fishing policy this country has seen. In view of their great differences over sealing, it would be only a Liberal policy which would bring those two together. Amazingly, it has done so.
On the east coast, the Hamilton Bank, the George's Bank and the Grand Bank portions of those major fishing areas are outside the 200-mile zone. Canada's position at the Law of the Sea conference was not 200 miles; it was 200 miles or the margin, whichever is the farthest. I think it is amazing that the minister today can introduce this statement without giving a single explanation of why the declaration did not include the margin on the east coast. Surely he has a

duty to this House to explain the discrepancy between the position taken by Alan Beesley and the fine Canadian delegation at the Law of the Sea conference and the position this government is now taking which is inconsistent with that position.
I hope the minister will spend a good deal of time in the question period trying to satisfy the House about this most serious discrepancy. I suspect it might have something to do with the treaty recently negotiated with the Soviet Union concerning the area outside the 200-mile zone. But, surely if the purpose of the declaration is to improve our negotiating stance at the ICNAF conference-and I suspect that is one of the reasons, and I suspect, by the way, that it could have been done two years ago and would have resulted in better fishing limits being established at that conference, but better late than never-now that the minister has made the declaration, how do we go to that conference with the margin open? Surely our hand would have been strengthened in June if we had gone for the margin and then negotiated from strength.
Again, it is a halfway position. We should have gone for the margin. We should have gone to the conference with strength, and then we could have reduced our fishing catches on the east coast. The date is significant. The date for implementation is January, 1977. The United States legislation will be effective in March, 1977.
It was assumed at the Law of the Sea conference that Canada would simply follow the United States, that its declaration would be effective shortly before the United States declaration, and that we would act under the umbrella in terms of the United States military strength to prevent a confrontation on the coast. But Mexico, for example, and Canada have different positions on the coast. The 200-mile zone meets the situation in respect of Mexico and the United States, but it does not meet the needs of Canada. I am amazed that the minister today would come forward with a declaration which is inconsistent with the right position which is the position Canada had taken at the Law of the Sea conference. Nevertheless, this is better late than never. We welcome the declaration. It is long overdue. This is a typical Liberal compromise on an important matter. I hope the minister will give immediate and serious reconsideration to the 200-mile zone and extend it to the edge of the margin on our east coast, where it belongs.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank the minister for having advised us ahead of time of the statement he intended to make at this time on our work on the 200-mile territorial limit.
As the other speakers from other parties of the opposition said so clearly and eloquently before me, in fact the minister made today a statement of intent on the general policy the government will adopt with regard to the protection of our coastline to a 200-mile limit. Mr. Speaker, in the final analysis, that is what it is. The minister recognizes it in his statement, and I quote:
There will be no fishery resource left if action is not taken now.
June 4, 1976

We are at least three years late in taking positive steps to protect our fisheries and encourage their development. In fact, nothing was done to preserve them either by the present Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) or by his predecessors. The minister said in his statement, he admits it implicitly, and I quote again:
Not only the fish but our Canadian fishermen too are an "endangered species", as I have heard them describe themselves.
The minister thus recognizes, Mr. Speaker, that this measure is not only late in coming but that it stands a chance of missing completely its objective, namely to stimulate the fishing industry in Canada and protect employment in fields related to that fundamental industry in the field of natural resources.
The minister is caught in some sort of diplomatic straightjacket, on the one hand in bilateral relations, the agreements signed with Norway, Poland, U.S.S.R., Portugal, Spain, and the United States-that is still to come- and on the other hand, in multilateral co-operation. On studying closely the statement of the minister and those of his predecessors on that technical and important topic, we note, Mr. Speaker, that the multilateral agreements, to come, and the co-operation will not be achieved tomorrow. In this regard, the minister says, once again:
New multilateral agreements will be needed to bring ... into line...
That is not done, Mr. Speaker, and the minister did not specify either in his statement whether or not he intends to take any action to achieve those multilateral agreements. All things considered, the minister recognizes now after three years that the government is late in taking any measures. He also recognizes that many fish species and especially the employment associated with the industry are both endangered, as he says.
The Minister also said that an order in council will be issued in 1977 which will establish the Canadian policy. But let us not be mistaken; it will be once again an order in council dealing within our own country limits and it will not necessarily make a success out of the policy announced by the government on preservation and bilateral or multilateral agreements.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, this is an excellent general statement of policy we are well accustomed to hear. It is well written but it does not, in the end, create a single job in the fishing industry nor insure any kind of investment for the preservation of fish species that are the main natural resource of this country. Further, we have no guarantee, no indication even, that the multilateral agreements to come will get a chance to succeed.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the minister emphasizes the importance of protecting these natural resources and I believe that every member and the whole world agree on that, but when the time comes to implement such an agreement, we will see whether our diplomats headed by the minister will be efficient enough to put it into action and see to it that our industry and our jobs will be protected.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in this field as in many others, for instance the textile industry, the shoe industry, I fear the government will take action when jobs will no longer be there. The government now allows into the country large quantities of foreign prod-
Fisheries
ucts, it does not do a thing about it, but just before election time, it will try to do something under the pretext that it wants to protect jobs that no longer exist.
The minister tells us now he will protect the industry that is nearly extinct. I think that what we need now is something more than pious assurances, but action to preserve these industries. Tomorrow may be too late.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously the case of the anadromous species is an important concern and has been an important objective of the Canadian delegation at the Law of the Sea conference which attempted, successfully, to ensure that the state of origin would have the principal responsibility for this resource. subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE
speechtext: My second question in the series has to do with those other elements which were in negotiation and what guarantees we are going to have, because they have an effect on fisheries. I am referring to the environmental element, the surface and subsurface navigation elements of an extension to 200 miles and the subsoil resources element of this proposition. It has been mentioned, but the extension of the edge of the margin is a very important one, too, and it was not included in the statement. So, is any provision going to be made with regard to jurisdiction over the environmental, surface and subsurface elements and the subsoil resources element?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE

As the hon. member realizes, under the international law, Canada already enjoys sovereign rights over the resources of the continental shelf. This includes mineral resources as well as the sedentary fish species on the shelf. Questions of the marine environment, scientific research-all important questions-are matters of further negotiation at the Law of the Sea conference.
The hon. member spoke about subsoil. I presume that the subsoil is included under mineral resources, but I will take further advice on that question. The hon. member referred to the question of the continental margin. It is true that

In the first place, the timing of the announcement today is related to some extent to the ICNAF meeting which is to take place next week in Montreal. At that meeting, the Canadian government will tell its partners that regulations which come into effect for 1977 must be in conformity with extended Canadian jurisdiction. It seemed to us that we ought to make that clear to our ICNAF partners and that we ought to make clear to the House today that that was our position.
I appreciate the commendation of the hon. member for the action we have taken. Obviously, we have all been wanting to take this action, but in my judgment we have

taken the action at just about the right time, not only because of the ICNAF meetings but because of the completed successful bilateral negotiations with the distant fishing states which will allow us to make what I consider to be a smooth transition to Canadian jurisdiction.
I realize that important fishery discussions with the United States are to take place in the future. It will be a major concern of mine that we reach satisfactory conclusions with the United States with respect to the boundary questions which exist with that country. I already communicated to Dr. Kissinger this morning the decision taken by the government of Canada and the necessity of taking a very serious attitude toward these bilateral negotiations between Canada and the United States. We have not yet completed our negotiations with France, but we do believe that it would be unrealistic, in view of the land base involved, for Canada to permit a 200-mile zone on the seaward side.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when beginning these remarks last Monday evening I was suggesting that there was growing concern in the country as to whether this chamber was capable of representing the views of Canadians in general. I am concerned that not all members will take the opportunity to debate this subject fully, particularly in view of the fact that the government House leader seems to think that 70 members having already participated is a rather extensive number.
I wish to speak for a few moments about the obligations of those of us who oppose the abolition of the death penalty. I believe that a member of the House of Commons has a greater duty to his constituents and the country than merely to get up at the appropriate time to cast a vote in this chamber, important as that may be. A member of the House of Commons has many obligations. He not only has an obligation to speak for his constituents, but for Canadians in general. In this particular case, a large number of members who oppose abolition of the death penalty are remaining silent. They are not participating in this debate. I urge hon. members to reconsider their position and speak in this debate before the second reading stage is concluded.
I am told that a number of people who want the abolition of capital punishment are not going to participate. They feel that if there is an early vote, the chances of success are greater. They believe that the longer it goes on, the less chance there is of the measure failing, as I believe it should. Those of us who oppose the abolition of capital punishment not only have a duty to our constituents but to many other Canadians whose voices will not be heard

June 4, 1976
Capital Punishment
through their member of this House. Over the years there have been a number of petitions, including a very large petition for a referendum on this subject. I have always felt that if there is one subject that is deserving of a referendum, it is that dealing with the retention or the abolition of capital punishment.
Most members on all sides of this House agree that it is a matter of conscience as to whether this should pertain. It is obvious that one member cannot reflect the conscience of everybody in his constituency. The government, of course, has been very stubborn with regard to allowing a referendum. They know that if this question is put to the people directly, the government's views will be soundly defeated. There is no question about that. Those of us who believe as the majority of Canadians believe, namely, that capital punishment should be retained, have an obligation to spin out this debate until the next election. That election could be something of a referendum on the subject we are considering. Indeed, that is the only reason we are discussing this issue.
The government has been completely dishonest in its approach. We have had a five-year period of abolition, commencing in 1967. In 1973 the government wanted the period extended by a further five years. At that time, the Solicitor General said it was only a second five-year period and that in the long run the government wanted a third before the question was finally decided. Of course, the second five-year period would ordinarily expire around the time of the next election. The reason the government is bringing this measure before the House now is that we are midway between elections: they want to get the question disposed of so that it will not be an issue in the next election.
To my mind, that is a dishonest approach because when the government brought forward Bill C-2 they said it would be the law for a certain period of time. Now they are asking us to change it again. We just cannot believe what the government says. The people are being denied the right to express themselves directly. Those of us who believe they ought to have that right should use every tactic and manoeuvre available to us to frustrate the will of the government on this matter, since the government does not have the people behind them. I hope everyone who favours the retention of capital punishment will exercise his right to speak and delay this measure so that it can become an issue at the time of the next election. If retentionists fail to do this, they are not being true to their professed stand; they are abusing their retentionist vote and regarding it as merely vote-gathering; they do not really believe retention is the proper thing. Even though I would agree with the way they vote, I cannot respect an hon. member who would do such a thing. At least the abolitionists are acting in the spirit of their conviction, but until I see all these retentionists speaking I question the spirit of their intentions; they may be simply bowing to the public will, and I do not think that is a good attitude for a member of this House to take.
As I say, the government has been dishonest in its approach to the whole subject. This is demonstrated by its failure to obey the law as parliament was asked to enact it. I understand that when Bill C-2 was brought in, an undertaking was given to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. 
Stanfield) that the government would obey the law. But they have broken their undertaking, as they have broken so many others.
I was opposed in the last election by a candidate who said the Liberal government had abolished capital punishment. That seemed to be the understanding of Liberal candidates, and that has certainly been the de facto situation because there has not been an execution in this country since 1962. The last major change in this area, before these experiments began in 1967, was in 1961 when the government of the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a significant change in the law, bringing in the distinction between capital and non-capital murder. There is no question that this was a great advance in the field of penology. But it has not had an opportunity to work, because only a year after the change in the law was made, the last execution took place and we have had de facto abolition ever since.
As far as the idea of a free vote is concerned, to my mind that is so much window-dressing. I am somewhat amazed to find the government suggesting an extension of hours to deal with this matter and only this matter. They want to extend the hours for the debate on capital punishment and get rid of it.

speechtext:
I am sure he would like to continue in them for a great length of time.
If this government really wanted to have a free vote on this subject, it could have adopted the procedure used in 1966 when the private members' route was used. If this government gave its blessing to a private members' motion or bill on this subject I am sure it would have got appropriate consideration in the House and we would not have had to worry about its being talked out or anything like that. The last time this procedure was used, I think six members of the administration voted for retention, including the Hon. John Turner. If the government were really sincere about having a truly free vote on this question, then this is the method that they would have adopted. Until they adopt such a procedure, Mr. Speaker, I question how free this vote is going to be. I think there is plenty of evidence to show that it is not.
As far as this whole so-called peace and security package is concerned-the government is afraid to call it a law and order package-the other element of dishonesty is the blatant bribe to members to pass the legislation in return for some very harsh and severe terms of imprisonment. The government is proposing a term of imprisonment of 25 years without any possibility of parole. If that were going to be the case, even the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) would feel compelled to vote against it. He does not really believe that the government is serious about this, though he certainly does not like what is being offered in this regard. It is clearly an out-and-out bribe to enable members to salve their consciences and support the government in this matter, in return for a very harsh, cruel, inhumane term of imprisonment.
Such a term of imprisonment is no bribe to me, because I do not think the government is honest anyway. It just is not honest, Mr. Speaker. What the government is offering now, it will start chipping away at later. We have had evidence of what the government wants to do in this area. We have heard the government's ideas about temporary absences, sending people off on trips, having people to go to Spain to get married, and so on. That is the government's idea of rehabilitation. Because of terrific public opposition to this sort of thing, the government is now changing its colour, like a chameleon. I suggest that if the House is foolish enough to fall for the government's proposal in this measure, within a year or two it will start chipping away at the term of imprisonment and we will end up with absolutely nothing.
If a convicted murderer does receive a 25 year mandatory sentence, we are told that after 15 years a panel of three judges could perhaps change the sentence so as to allow for parole. I think statistics now show that the average capital murderer is released from jail after 13.2 years. If, under the new law, he is paroled after 15 years, all we have added is 1.8 years, which to me is not that significant. There has been this great foofaraw about a 25-year maximum term. I do not think it is true about the 15 years, because if it were the government would lose support. Nevertheless, it is a poor show for the government to resort to this type of bribery in addition to all the other chicanery it has engaged in on this subject.
As far as my own constituency is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I have conducted a couple of polls and it is quite clear

June 4, 1976
Capital Punishment
where my constituents stand, which I suppose makes my job easy since in no way would I be in opposition to the vast bulk of my constituents. In 1971, 76 per cent were in favour of capital punishment, 20 per cent said no, and 4 per cent were undecided. In 1973, 79.4 per cent favoured capital punishment, 18.4 per cent said no, and 2.2 per cent were undecided. In the latter poll I also asked whether, if life really was life, they would have a different view; 41.7 per cent said they would; 54.2 per cent said that they still wanted capital punishment even if life was life.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Even if life meant life it was not satisfactory to 54.2 per cent of my constituents; they still felt capital punishment should be retained. Much of this has to do with the situation in our penitentiaries. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has also said that in order to protect society we shall have to improve the situation in our penitentiaries; that there will be great reforms. We have been having great reforms in our penitentiaries for 15 years or more, Mr. Speaker, starting when Alan MacLeod began the new wave of penal reform. I do not know what kind of reform we are achieving in view of the sort of situation that has arisen in the B.C. penitentiary. I should like to read a couple of paragraphs by Doug Collins which appeared in the Toronto Star for April 30 last and had to do with that institution. He said this:
The B.C. penitentiary, that grim, ancient, shabby and hopeless pile in New Westminster, has to be the laughingstock of the country. Hostagetaking now seems to be taking place every week, prisoners demand flights to everywhere and sometimes get them (in exchange for a guard who in return doesn't get his throat cut) and there is a general atmosphere of what-will-happen-next?
What will happen next, if those close to the scene know anything, is that the place will explode. Concessions to the violent lead to more concessions, guards hate prisoners, prisoners hate guards, and everyone-guards, prisoners and public alike-hates Ottawa, which is supposed to control this mess.
It is obvious that the government cannot deal with this situation. Instead of discussing this bill we should be getting down to the root of the problem in our penal system. If the government can show us there is no hope for our penal system, then maybe some of us would be obliged to change our minds; but surely at this time there is no argument for changing one's mind in respect of the retention of capital punishment.
In a little over a month the Olympic Games will be commencing in Montreal. We are spending some $30 million, $40 million or $50 million for security there, and we are being warned all the time that terrorists may be coming in from outside this country who will take disruptive action at the games. Our immigration procedures are being tightened, along with the United States regulations to protect against this. All sorts of things are being done. I wonder what the attitude among terrorists in the world would be if two or three weeks before the opening of the Olympics, Canada abolished the death sentence. Surely that would give some support to the idea that we are not really as serious about this subject as we ought to be. If for no other reason than that one alone, we should be postponing the conclusion of this legislation. It should wait until the fall before coming to a decision.

Let me return again to what I was saying about our penitentiary system. It is quite obvious, from some of Mr. Collins' comments, that the system is out of control in British Columbia and in some other places in the country. I might point out that the penitentiary located at my place of residence, Drumheller, Alberta, has been called the gem of the system. It certainly creates the least problems. I know there are problems there, but they have not got out of control as they have in other places in the country. We are very fortunate and I am very proud of the staff of that institution because they have worked things out very well. However, if we are to continue with the sloppy way in which the government is dealing with our penal system, I am afraid that even the situation at Drumheller will deteriorate.
I, for one, feel that in order to keep the situation in these institutions under control we must pay more attention to what has been said by the director of the B.C. penitentiary and others across this country. They feel they should be able to use the paddle to effect some sort of discipline and order in these institutions. It is intolerable when the inmates run the institutions. That is just not acceptable. Instead of following this advice, the government is continually chipping away at the effectiveness of punishment in this country, whether in the institutions or outside.
I do not like to be critical of my friends of the New Democratic Party, particularly when there is no one representing them in the House at this moment, but I find it rather unusual that such a democratic party can be so united in its opposition to the death penalty when such a large proportion of its grassroots supporters in the country favour retention.
Dr. Fattah, criminologist at the Simon Fraser University, who has been referred to by some as the high priest of abolition in this country, carried out a study on behalf of the Solicitor General regarding support for this measure in various party groups. Of course, the supporters of the Social Credit party in Canada are the strongest in favour of maintaining the death penalty, followed by the Conservative party and the Liberals. However, even in the NDP a substantial number of people want the death penalty retained. The latest figures in the study are for 1971, and they show that 43.75 per cent of NDP supporters want the death penalty retained. That is a significant number and I wonder how, among 16 here, there is not at least one who would speak on behalf of that element of that party. I find this very unusual, and I think it should be commented on by the grassroots of that party to its parliamentary membership.
Popular belief would have it that everyone in the NDP in this country is opposed to capital punishment. That is not true. In 1960, when it was the CCF party, 61.1 per cent felt that capital punishment should not be abolished-and that is only 16 years ago. These are national figures. Someone in the NDP should explain why their parliamentary group is so opposed to capital punishment, contrary to the belief of a great many of their grassroots members. That is not very democratic at all.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to know that the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) will explain that later today.
Many people have suggested we cannot have capital punishment because there is one law for the rich and one for the poor. I think the teeth of that argument were pulled long ago. We have a tremendous legal aid system in this country now, supported by millions of dollars. From my own experience in Alberta, there is never a shortage of funds to hire proper counsel to make sure that justice is done in this area-so that argument just does not apply.
In conclusion, let me suggest that the law after 1961 was never allowed to function. Some still argue this matter on the basis that people who kill as a result of passion will be hanged. That is not the law. The law as it was passed in 1961 is that capital punishment shall be reserved for those people who, on a planned and deliberate basis, or on a contract basis, go out and murder somebody, or kill somebody in the commission of a planned and deliberate criminal offence. That is not in any way, shape or form a crime of passion. So that argument is completely meaningless.
Capital punishment is a deterrent to those who might otherwise set out on a deliberate plan or course of action that would likely result in somebody's death. Human nature is such that individuals place great value on their lives and people are not going to do something that will likely threaten them. I agree that capital punishment does not have much deterrent effect in respect of those who may commit crimes of passion, but this is not the law and that is not what we are arguing. We are suggesting capital punishment for those who deliberately plan murder. Those people should not have the ghost of a chance of ever doing the same thing again.
I urge all hon. members to participate in this very important debate and use every means at their disposal to make sure the real feelings of the Canadian people are expressed, whether right or wrong. If the Canadian people are wrong, we will have the opportunity to correct them. In the meantime, there are a great many families and dependants of victims to whom we have a duty. We cannot confine our thoughts or considerations to those who have actually taken somebody else's life; we have a greater duty than that.

Mr. Speaker, the numbers present this afternoon would indicate that Friday is not a vintage day among all parties for attendance in the House of Commons. I mention that, not by way of criticism but simply to point out the fact that I am informed discussions are now taking place concerning the enlargement of this House because of the increase of members that will follow the acceptance of the new redistribution measure. Indeed, Your Honour, the throne will be moved back some distance. I suggest there be no increase in the size.
One reason for the power of the parliament of Westminster in so far as the House of Commons is concerned is that the membership cannot always find seats, benches, on which to sit and the result is there is a feeling of urgency. Indeed, when I was prime minister I endeavoured to bring
Capital Punishment
about a change. I had fairly good support, but one would require general support to remove the desks and substitute benches. However, the quality of debate in this House would multiply very greatly. Now that the House is to be increased in size, I suggest there be something done along the line of not increasing the size but of providing benches at the back for those members who are not present and therefore cannot occupy seats. When people visit the gallery and see the House of Commons virtually unoccupied, there is no greater criticism offered than that when they return home. However, that afternoon he said, "Oh, I was just musing". Musings of that kind with the life of individuals at stake on the part of anyone are not amusing. Then later on, when faced with the fact that overwhelmingly across Canada there is a demand for capital punishment for murder, he said, "Well, if public opinion is aroused, then I guess we will have to have a few hangings". That, to me, is not the kind of statement that is in keeping with the seriousness of the question that we face.
We find that not only was the legislation passed in 1973 to be repealed, but a further section has been included in the bill to abolish the death sentence for treason. I ask the government: what group of Canadians have asked that it be abolished for treason? Certainly, it has not been the organizations that ordinarily deal with civil liberties. Nowhere, at any time, has any organized or unorganized group in this country asked the government to abolish what is accepted everywhere in the world as the punishment for treason. Why is it included? When I suggested to the Prime Minister that he withdraw that, he became very petulant, peevish-not unusual today-and then he became annoyed with the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather), very annoyed with him. Why? Why is the gov-

ernment, in 1976, bringing in legislation of this kind, when during the summer at any time, and particularly I emphasize during the present summer, from all parts of the world people will gather for the Olympics?
I will read to hon. members the law as it is now, so that there will be no mistake about it. This law has been on the statute books for years. The Canadian Civil Liberties Organization has not asked that the law regarding treason be repealed. Again I challenge the government to name one organization or anyone of responsibility across Canada who has asked for this. The sections in question should be placed on the record. Sections 46 and 47 at present read as follows:
46(1) Every one commits treason who, in Canada
(a)	kills or attempts to kill Her Majesty, or does her any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, maims or wounds her, or imprisons or restrains her;
(b)	levies war against Canada or does any act preparatory thereto;
(c)	assists an enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities ...
(d)	uses force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada or a province;
(e)	without lawful authority, communicates or makes available to an agent of a state other than Canada, military or scientific information or any sketch, plan, model, article, note or document of a military or scientific character that he knows or ought to know may be used by that state for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or defence of Canada...
47(1) Every one who commits treason is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable
(a) To be sentenced to death if he is guilty of an offence under paragraph 46(l)(a), (b) or (c)-
That is the killing or the attempted killing of the Queen of Canada, to levy war against Canada or to assist an enemy at war with Canada. Why has this been changed at this time? Nobody has answered that. Again I repeat: there is something gratuitous about the government's action in this regard. Then so far as penalties are concerned, if all one does is to use force or violence for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Canada or a province, they may be sentenced to death or to imprisonment for life.
There is something behind this, and that is what we have not found out. What has activated the government of Canada to bring before the House legislation which will make Canada an open place for assassination and treason subject only to a jail sentence in a world in which terrorism marches and assassinations and kidnappings with assassination take place all over the world? Just at this time the government of Canada decides that it must be kind to terrorists, international murderers and those who raise rebellion.
I ask those who, together with me, believe that so far as murder is concerned as an offence against the individual- and of course an offence against the state-it should not be punished by the death sentence. I ask those who believe in the abolition of capital punishment, how can they, in their own conscience, vote for this bill which contains the particular clauses to which I have referred? The parliament of Great Britain has abolished the death penalty for murder. I have the bill here, which is entitled, "Abolition of the Death Penalty Act". In the observations made thereon, the following appears:
June 4, 1976

Sentence of death can still and only be awarded for high treason, piracy with violence-
And one or two other offences.
-when a person is convicted of treason, sentence of death must be pronounced.
Why at this time, with the law in effect that the government of Canada stated three years ago was the epitome of all legal perfection, is the government changing this law? I said it would not work, dividing murder according to the occupation of the victim. I voted for it because, as I pointed out, half a loaf is better than none. I said it would not work. It is still in effect and will be in effect until December of 1977. Why, then, this sudden rush, this haste on the part of the government, to force through parliament before this session ends something that carries with it the possibility that each of us can imagine?
As one who, as prime minister, had this responsibility, I know what it means to sign the death sentence. That is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the acting prime minister in his absence has to do by way of a recommendation to the Governor General of Canada. I know what it means. When I was prime minister if there were any reasonably extenuating circumstances, commutation took place, but when there was no such justification, the sentence was carried out. The last two who went to the gallows in this country went on an order or a direction signed by me. The law was enforced until the present government started playing around with the problem, and since then no one has been executed. Today there is almost a platoon of individuals in our institutions waiting, waiting and wondering what is going to happen.
Why the ungodly haste to bring in this legislation at this time? This House has been sitting now since September of 1974, the longest session in all history and the nearest approach to parliamentary eternity ever seen in our country. And here at the last moment this bill comes along, and we must pass it or continue to sit. Why?
I mentioned a moment ago that the Canadian Civil Liberties Association did not ask for this. Nowhere in its statement of conscience, signed by many of the most responsible of Canadians, is there any question of abolition for other than murder.
I have read these sections of the bill. When I first found out, I could not believe that the Government of Canada in this year-or any year, but this year particularly-would bring in this legislation. Happy days are here again for terrorists all over the world, for those who would destroy, and for those who would undermine the Government of Canada. Am I overstating it?

I am not making a partisan speech today. I am making one from the heart, regardless of whether somebody may say I am guilty of inconsistency. Not at all, for I repeat, treason is treason. I can just see Castro-because he has become somewhat of a highly regarded individual in some parts of our country by some people-sending some of his 12,000 up here. Could we stop them? There are some in this country who are so fond of Castro that they go to see him face to face. He tried to see me in 1962, and I was busy, but there are others who found it necessary to endeavour to visit him by canoe. They did not get there. Greater love hath no man than he who would endanger his life in a canoe to get to Cuba.
Under this legislation a group of individuals in Canada who want to set up a Marxist state by force can do so, but subject to what? A comparatively short period of imprisonment! That is my first and main point. I will be back. I have to be away because I did not expect that parliament would be sitting for so long. Nobody else did either. The reason parliament today in large measure is in contempt across Canada is the fact that it is being used as a plaything. We sit, we talk for an hour and ask questions-as does the hon. member who interrupted me earlier, but our questions are more intelligent than his-and then what happens? The House sits and goes on. Unless every one of us begins to realize the feeling of the Canadian people, I fear for the future of a free parliament, for everywhere in the world history shows that democratic countries go under when citizens begin to lose faith in their democratic leaders.

June 4, 1976
Capital Punishment
I can understand the attitude of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). He is widely criticized. He carries the mark of Cain on him, but he is doing what the government requires that he do within the powers which are granted to him. He is frank about it. He has withdrawn his suggestion that if this bill passes, he is out-with one change; he has said he will be out of the cabinet to start with. Now he has said, "I should like another portfolio".
Sir, no vote will be more important than this one. I am not going to draw a frightening picture of July, 1976, at the Olympics but I am telling you that unless a fraud is being perpetrated on the Canadian people by the government in contending that we have to spend, among the two or three levels of government, approximately $1 million on security-if that is so, then by passing this bill we are placing ourselves in the position of accessories before the fact. This is dangerous. To take such a course at any time would be dangerous but to do it now-Mr. Speaker, I do not want to express how much I fear the consequences.
Some suggestions have been made that we will pass the bill and put it into committee. I know there are some worshippers of committee in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Mr. Speaker, I have been here longer than most and I believe that many wish that had not taken place, but I have formed opinions. Committees are fine when they are dealing with matters that are non-partisan, are simple inquiries. Is there any member of this House who would say that if he were on the committee, regardless of what others would do, he would insist on the removal of this portion that has no place in it whatsoever?
Some people ask what will happen if the bill is defeated. Well, until December, 1977, the law will still be in effect. The government brought it in and said it was the nearest thing to Utopia in criminal procedure; it was going to bring about a new heaven and a new earth. Now that a lineup of individuals is awaiting execution, the government insists that this be passed. What will be the result, Mr. Speaker? If it is passed, we simply pass back to the government its responsibilities under the law. I am not here to say there should be no commutations-nothing of the kind. The matter of commutation naturally rests with the exercise of the Queen's mercy. No government should permit itself to be forced into a position to execute anyone simply by the force of public opinion.
All we will do if we defeat the bill because of the insertion of this reprehensible clause is give the government back the responsibility that it assumed in 1973 of deciding whether an individual shall live or die. Send it to the committee? We may just as well stand on our heads and expect to be effective in the House of Commons as to bring about the removal of that clause through a committee.
Other people ask where we go from here. That is not for us to say, Mr. Speaker. No one in this House of Commons, to my knowledge, has ever discussed the abolition of capital punishment for treason. We should defeat the bill, set up a committee and hear evidence in that place. It is as simple as can be.
Sir, I was going to say much more. I shall not do so. I am an abolitionist by conscience and by experience. One time

Churchill was taking a stand which was believed to be inconsistent, and he was charged with it. He said, "I have no defence against the charge except when events change, principles sometimes have to change".
Bring in the bill without that clause and I will vote for it. Bring it in in its present form and make Canada the Mecca-if I may use that expression in this oil world-for all the thugs, terrorists, PLOs and Castros. As for me, my conscience will be clear when I vote against it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the arguments for and against the abolition of capital punishment have been debated in this Chamber and in many other legislative bodies in many countries throughout the world. In spite of the millions of words that have been spoken, we still have murders committed in countries with capital punishment and in countries where the death penalty has been abolished. And, Mr. Speaker, the commission of murder will continue regardless of the outcome of this debate. Man is not a rational being, he is only capable of reason. And man is not a perfect being either, so his imperfections and weaknesses will continue. The point is, how best do we control man's imperfections in the interests of law and order, safety and security for the great majority who live within the law?
I am an abolitionist because my conscience tells me that violence begets violence and that the state should not lower itself to the level of its most wretched citizens. This of course is a very personal and subjective argument. I make no claim that my conscience is any more pure or moral than the consciences of those in this House who support capital punishment. Indeed I will make no attempt to persuade hon. members to accept my point of view. We must all stand and be counted as individuals when the vote is recorded.
What I will attempt to do is to explain why I am an abolitionist, in full knowledge of the fact that a majority of my constituents want capital punishment at this time-I emphasize that last phrase-at this time. I am also aware that should the voters of Brant at the next election choose to appraise my work on this single issue, I may not return to the House of Commons. This is the chance that I and other abolitionists must take in the free spirit of parliamentary democracy.
I mentioned that my support for abolition of the death penalty was based on my conscience. This certainly is not the only reason, because if I thought that the evidence with respect to capital punishment clearly showed that this kind of cruel and unusual punishment was in fact a deterrent to the commission of murder, or other crimes of violence, I would on this issue accept those facts and vote for retention.
I would now like to look at the evidence we have all studied over the last three and a half years which, I suggest to hon. members, most Canadians outside this Chamber have not studied thoroughly.
First I should like to state, as other have thus far, that concentrating on the issue of capital punishment will do

little to protect Canadians from increases in the over-all crime that is occurring in this country. People who have written letters with regard to capital punishment have not only expressed their fear and concern about murder. They have also made it known that they are equally appalled about robberies, attempted murders, assaults, sexual offences, as well as other crimes.
We note, for example, that 1974 assaults accounted for 75 per cent of all violent crimes. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) stated in his opening remarks in this debate that unless we are prepared to exact the death penalty for those who indulge in assaults, then those who argue that capital punishment is the only effective deterrent available will be leaving aside as much as 80 per cent of all other violent crimes. Keeping this in mind there can be no doubt that the re-institution of capital punishment would be totally inadequate as a means of dealing with the total crime scene in this country.
I am reminded of a statistical report on crime prepared by the city police force of Brantford, Ontario, in my constituency, Crime in that city rose 25.8 per cent in 1975 over 1974. Obviously, citizens there are concerned and rightly so, and so am I. If one looks at the types of crimes committed, it becomes evident that either retaining or abolishing capital punishment would have absolutely no effect on this since none of these would be punishable by death.
Break-ins, fraud, theft, and assault accounted for most of the increased crime in the city of Brantford. By and large these are the types of crimes citizens are concerned with, and I reiterate that concentrating on the issue of capital punishment will not provide us with a means of dealing with over 75 per cent of our crimes.
This having been said, I would like to return to the specific question of whether capital punishment acts as a deterrent. I believe that in order to analyse fully the deterrent or non-deterrent aspects of capital punishment we must not only look at the statistics of murder but also the nature of the acts committed and of the people who committed them.
Paul Reid has studied this subject extensively and, in a paper entitled "Murder in Canada", he states that most murders are committed at home by people who have been drinking. Furthermore, the weapon most used in the 545 murders committed in Canada last year was a gun, most often a rifle or a shotgun. Fewer than 11 per cent of the deaths occurred during the commission of another criminal act such as rape, robbery or arson, while 36.3 per cent involved domestic relationships.
This study, as others before it did, suggests that, generally speaking, murder is not the deliberate act of the hardened criminal but rather an impulsive, irrational, unthinking deed either by an average citizen momentarily impassioned, or by the mentally unbalanced. If we accept this analysis it becomes clear that the vast majority of murders usually involve passion and little thought is given to the possible punishment.
Numerous other studies have been done which suggest that capital punishment is not a deterrent. In the United States, U.S. criminologist Thorsten Sellin found that there were no real differences in homicide rates between states that had and had not capital punishment. Sellin also noted
Capital Punishment
that there was no upsurge of murder in states which had abolished capital punishment, nor was there any real decline in states where it was restored.
Professor Sellin's conclusions were found in earlier years by the British Royal Commission studying capital punishment. The commission found, and I quote:
-there is no clear evidence in any of the figures we have examined that the abolition of capital punishment had led to an increase in the homicide rate or that its re-introduction had led to a fall.
It is interesting to note that not long ago in the British House of Commons, which represents 48 million to 50 million people in the United Kingdom, where there has been a lot of terrorism and brutal murders in northern Ireland, bombings in London, Liverpool, Manchester and other places, in their wisdom they overwhelmingly rejected the re-instatement of capital punishment.
Going back even further in time we find that in nineteenth century England-I know this example has been worn threadbare, but it is still relevant-pickpockets were hanged in public yet the best time for a pickpocket to carry out his trade was during a public hanging.
This relates to another issue which bothers me to a considerable degree. If we brought back capital punishment for first degree murder-
