speechtext: We have it now.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
-after 15 or 20 people have been hanged, juries may become extremely reluctant to bring in a verdict of first degree murder when in fact the murder was first degree. They will bring in a verdict of second degree murder simply because they are by nature abolitionists. As happened during the fifties, society will get tired of the responsibility of having to declare that someone should forfeit his life. Retentionists should keep in mind that within five years' time this could conceivably happen. People will get very upset, and jurors will let a man off for first degree and convict for second degree. Instead of spending 25 years in jail that person would be out much sooner as a result of a lesser conviction.
In Canada the most noted study on this subject, compiled by Ezzat A. Fattah of Simon Fraser University, again suggests, and I quote:
-that the cause of homicide and murder cannot be found in any single factor but in a total situation in which a special law or particular punishment can have little or no effect.
The professor also pointed out that:
-other offences of violence for which there has not been a change in punishment should show no increase or at least a lower increase than that in criminal homicide.
In other words, to those who argue that the suspension of a particular type of punishment leads to an increase in a category of crime, I would simply ask, for instance, why the rate of assaults in a city like Brantford has increased dramatically? Obviously the sentencing in 1975 was no different than in 1974.
I have become convinced that capital punishment is not the solution to lessening murder rates. An examination of the evidence that I have presented today, as well as of evidence provided by other members and specialists outside this Chamber, indicates that capital punishment does not effectively lower the murder rate.
14180

June 4, 1976
Capital Punishment
In dealing with this matter we must also necessarily deal with the irreversibility of the death penalty. While it may rarely occur, there is that possibility of error in our judicial system. Professor Charles Black in his book "Capital Punishment: The Inevitability of Caprice and Mistake" concludes that, aside from the moral implications, capital punishment should not be instituted because of the vulnerability of the criminal justice system to caprice and mistake. Hon. members cannot ignore this on the basis of the odds involved. Even if one innocent person is hanged, it is the mistake of those in this House. A brief review of the empirical or factual evidence leads me to believe that you cannot support capital punishment on deterrent grounds.
I have noticed that in some of the speeches given by hon. members capital punishment has been supported and refuted on the basis of moral arguments. While I don't intend to indulge in a moral or philosophical approach to this topic I would like to deal briefly with the religious authorities which some have used to support the retention of the death penalty. I do this because much of my mail on the subject cites the Scriptures in favour of capital punishment.
It has been pointed out, not only by the Solicitor General but by other members as well, that narrow scripture citations can be used to support almost any point of view. In this regard I would simply like to quote what my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The-Islands (Mr. Douglas), had to say about using the Scripture on this subject:
The Bible has been quoted in times past to support slavery, child-labour, polygamy, and burning of witches. Furthermore the Mosaic law provided at one time the death penalty for over 30 crimes, including adultery, homosexuality and witchcraft.
Obviously use of Scriptures out of context should not be emphasized in this debate. Let us not play God.
The main concern, indeed, our main task during this debate, is to determine whether capital punishment-its retention-will resolve our problems with crime, not only violent murder but all crime. I mentioned at the outset of my remarks that most people who have written to me on the subject of capital punishment fear for their own as well as their children's safety. What they read in the papers daily and what they see on their television nightly is frightening them. Yet much of this may be overplayed.
There has been some evidence presented in the House to suggest that the media has heightened the public's perception of its own safety. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) as well as my colleague from New Westminster have cited an article in the April edition of Psychology Today which indicated that one of the effects of violence on television is to create a perception in people's minds whereby they believe the violence they see on TV is like the real world around them. It is worth while quoting from the conclusions drawn from the article. The article states:
We have found that violence on prime time network TV cultivates exaggerated assumptions about the threat of danger in the real world. This may lead to increasing demands for protection and to increasing pressure for the use of force by the established authority.
The same conclusions have been reached by Hans Mohr, a criminologist, who in 1969 became the first non-lawyer

appointed as a full-time faculty member of the Osgoode Law School. For two years Mr. Mohr was also a member of the Law Reform Commission. In a recent interview with Quest magazine Mr. Mohr said that the incidence of crime isn't quite as high as some would have us believe. The situation, he says, is exaggerated by society in general and by the media in particular. He says:
Communication is so good today that we seem to hear about everything. If we live in Vancouver we hear about a murder in Toronto. If we're in Charlottetown we know about a killing in Victoria. The important thing is that this is all we hear.
What he refers to here is that we rarely hear about the nature of the crime committed, something I mentioned earlier. For instance we may get a story on the late night news that a murder has been committed, but what we don't learn is that it was a husband who shot his wife while they were both drunk. Mr. Mohr concludes, "We don't find out that this is not the sort of murder that is very likely to threaten our own lives".
I do not mean to infer that crime in our society is no less a serious problem that it was five or ten years ago. As in my own riding, crimes of all kinds are on the increase. Yet we have to realize that this debate, focusing narrowly as it does on a form of punishment for approximately 10 per cent of our crime, will do little to deal with the other 90 per cent of criminal offences.
I believe that the sizeable majority of those in this country who favour capital punishment simply want to be assured of their safety. I share this concern for safety. We must ensure that parole boards do not grant temporary paroles or temporary leaves to prisoners if their release would pose a threat to society at large. We must also ensure that those who are in prison remain there-in other words, that our prison system is secure. Bail reform must be structured in such a manner that bail is not granted to those whose release may be dangerous to society.
More important, the whole Criminal Code needs to be reviewed to ensure that punishment serves a purpose. In one of the Law Reform Commission Reports it was found that four out of seven offenders in crimes involving property went to jail for a first offence. Most of us here must surely find that intolerable. The Commission concluded that society would be better served by a system of 'diversion', i.e. a method whereby offenders and victims are given the opportunity to find their own solutions instead of having the state impose a sentence in each and every case. This type of system could be used in cases where there is a good chance that the offender will not commit another crime. As criminologist Hans Mohr stated:
What we need most... is a change in the public attitude toward punishment, away from the idea of harsh sentences, with no real purpose. When someone commits a crime you have to look at two things: What caused the crime? How do you punish it-and what will the punishment accomplish?
Finally we must direct most of our energy to finding the root causes of crime within our society. It has been said before, but needs to be reaffirmed, that hanging is a simplistic response which may satisfy our understandable desire for vengeance and safety but does nothing to solve the problem of violence and crime.
June 4, 1976

I would like to end my brief remarks in this debate by quoting Hans Mohr once more. This last quotation summarizes my feelings towards capital punishment. He said:
I would not be against it if it did any good, if it prevented murder. But there is absolutely no indication that it does. And I cannot see the sense in trying to prevent the killing of people by killing other people.
I mentioned earlier that juries were reluctant to convict anyone of first degree murder because they are either abolitionists or are simply tired of seeing society or the government take a life for a life. I want to end on one or two more notes. I refer to capital punishment as cruel and unusual punishment, a phrase which comes, I believe, from one of the amendments to the U.S. Constitution. I believe it to be so. I also believe that 25 years in jail is an equally cruel and unusual punishment. There is absolutely no incentive toward rehabilitation regardless of that 15-year time span in which a convicted murderer may petition three Superior Court judges and then, hopefully, go to the Parole Board and perhaps in the next few years be released. Twenty-five years behind penitentiary bars, in this country at least, is probably a punishment worse than death.
What I would like to suggest, and I know it is not novel, is that the hardened criminal, the criminal who refuses to try to rehabilitate himself and be receptive to rehabilitation programs within the penitentiary system, should be forced to work at meaningful jobs in extreme protective custody. I would suggest that such prisoners be paid and that part of their money be banked, the money to go to supporting their families, if they have them, and toward defraying the cost of their own support instead of forcing the taxpayers to pay the whole load.
Speaking now of the hardened criminal, the hit man, the contract killer, if there is one thing that these people are absolutely terrified of it is an honest, hard day's work, because they have never lived that way in their lives; they have lived by crime. It is doubtful that this will ever get to committee, but I would suggest that some day this provision be incorporated into the 25 year or 20 year life sentence. The government is proposing 25 years now, but it may be 30 years at some point in time or it may be reduced to 20 years. Simply to lock these people up and keep them in prison like animals is inhumane. So I reiterate and re-emphasize that, as an abolitionist, I suggest the government consider getting these people out of the penitentiary for at least eight or 10 hours a day and putting them to meaningful work, which would be the toughest punishment for them but would not be inhumane.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to me this debate on capital punishment is very important. It is also troubling, for a reason I would like to explain.
We have now before us some very specific legislation reflecting the intentions either of cabinet as a whole or of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and his advisers. This bill was not prepared and written under the influence of members but rather some expert types who prepared it
95568-631/2

June 4, 1976
Capital Punishment
according to their knowledge and opinions. This means we have to decide on a very specific bill that does not necessarily reflect the views of members on the crime situation in Canada and the treatment of criminals.
I would like to put on record that by conscience I cannot favour capital punishment. But as a member of Parliament,
I have received a mandate from my constituency. I hope therefore I reflect the opinion of one part of this country. I will therefore endeavour to see beyond my own conscience and my own views, to evaluate in the fairest and most objective way I can the crime situation in Canada, in the light of which I will make a judgement on the specific legislation introduced by the Solicitor General.
Under this bill, we would abolish capital punishment once and for all, and replace it by 25 years' imprisonment for some kinds of murders. The bill explains the various kind of murders. They call this peace and security, this bill respecting the control of firearms and capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, as the member for Lotbiniere, I cannot support the bill. I am forced by my conscience to vote with those who want to retain capital punishment, for the reasons I shall explain.
There are five factors around which this debate should be centered. First of all, everyone in the House will recognize that there is a serious increase in the crime rate in Canada. This is not restricted to one province or one area, but is generalized. We can look at the hearings of Quebec's Commission of Inquiry into Organized Crime and see how criminal organized forces in a premeditated, organized and even super-organized manner, direct operations which are not only illegal, but also murderous for their own profit. It is a kind of parallel government or power. It controls the automobile market, prostitution, thieving, and so on. This is the first fact that everyone will admit.
The second fact is the one which concerns me most, is spite of the fine statements of principle of the Solicitor General who, to this date, has been satisfied with making statements. Action is still not for today, it seems. Juvenile delinquency in Canada is still seriously increasing and directly related with the crime rate. What about probation, assistance and support programs for young people who have committeed only one offence, which is not necessarily criminal? What are we doing to help these young people rehabilitate themselves? Very often they commit offences of this type because of an unbalanced or unsteady family context or because of money, education or schooling However, this minister who is asking us to abolish the death penalty has done absolutely nothing concrete to prevent crime among young people and to help them.
Fourth everyone will once again admit that the penitentiary system in Canada is completely inadequate. People go in and come out constantly, and we are no longer surprised in Canada that someone can go to prison, be released, go back in and come back out again. This happens constantly. A criminal is arrested and has a trial which costs a lot of money. The criminal is set up comfortably in prison, in spite of what some of my colleagues will say, and the first thing we know is that he has been released. When he does not get out by himself, it is with the help of the Solicitor General through the National Parole Board. And the criminal regains his freedom.

In this respect, Mr. Speaker, the National Parole Board is mainly responsible for the great concern of the public as regards the crime rate. The minister tells us: believe me, if you want us to abolish the death penalty, I promise you that we will not grant paroles in such or such a case and that we shall be very strict. This is what he says, but in the same breath, he says that if we do not approve his bill, he will resign. This is blackmail and it distorts the debate; there can no longer be a free vote under these conditions. Those who want the Solicitor General to resign will certainly vote against the bill and those who want him to stay will vote for it. Mr. Speaker, I think we should consider these factors during the debate on the death penalty. To abolish the death penalty, we would need not only the assurance but also the promise, within the framework of a very specific program that we would make assessments to control the crime rate in Canada. What methods shall we use? What shall we do? It's very nice, Mr. Speaker, to watch on Quebec TV criminals appearing before the inquiry commission, it is very entertaining. But what does it change to organized crime? What safeguards do we give to the public?
Mr. Speaker, this is a first point on which the Solicitor General shall decide once and for all. What does he intend to do to control organized crime in Canada? We do not have any answer on that subject. The minister is a staunch abolitionist but he proposes absolutely nothing to control and contain the increase in crime. It is absolutely essential and with an example I will illustrate this attitude that I cannot understand, this lack of action on the part of the government.
A criminal commits an armed robbery in a jewelry. The police is called. Policemen are paid for this as it is their function, their work to defend and protect the life and the property of the public. In Canada, policemen are armed. So they arrive on the scene of the robbery and there, Mr. Speaker, they risk their life instead of the owner if he is not there to prevent the robbery. The thieves went there not empty handed but with arms in a premeditated manner. So they chose a course of action. They developed a strategy. So they go to carry out their robbery and they are armed in case society should try to prevent them from doing so because, according to them, they have the right to take someone else's property. There are lots of laws in Canada against theft, but in the mind of those hardened criminals it is not a theft. I do not refer to the one who commits a crime of jealousy or non-premeditated offences, I refer to the organized criminal who commits a robbery. It is premeditated. He intends to take someone else s property.
I believe that in Canada we still recognize the right to private property. Society pays policemen to prevent that kind of incidents. What does happen? If policemen arrive on the scene of the crime, obviously shots will be fired. Why? Because someone wanted to earn his living honourably through his work and someone else decided not to work and not to live honourably by robbing the property of the one who works honestly all day long. This is a theft.
Such a theft is usually made by someone who refuses to proceed in the normal way to get an income and wants to take advantage of the income of another who has worked and took some pains to earn one. Then, Mr. Speaker, the

policeman risks his life to protect and prevent such an action. The thief who is caught or taken by surprise takes flight, trying to save his skin. For the policeman, it is self-defence since he is on duty. This is why he wears a uniform, he is armed and trained.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, two things might happen after such a hypothetical incident. The policemen finally catch the criminal or the thief who is tried and with supporting evidence is finally jailed. Then the Solicitor General intervenes after merely a few years. The statistics are there to show that the same thief is caught back and discharged again. Such a thing happens.
When gun shots have been exchanged, Mr. Speaker, and a police agent has been injured, and I know at least two who are completely paralysed, who will be incapacitated for life, and a third who is all crippled following an act committed while on duty, it is therefore a premeditated murder. Some might say, it is an accident, that it derives from the theft. That is the argument put forward by my predecessor from the NDP-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Lake-shore (Mr. Robinson) for his efforts on behalf of a large number of Canadians. There is no doubt that the hon. member who sponsors this bill is doing so on the basis of kindness and consideration for others. If you prefer, he would seem to be placing the well-being of others before one's self. I am sure non-smokers, particularly those who suffer from asthma, emphysema, or a similar ailment, are grateful to the hon. member for his efforts to enable them to travel in comfort. In some cases people are unable to travel because of the effect of smoke in a confined area.
I believe we should stop to consider how this bill, if it should pass, could be administered. Would a passenger, whether on a bus, a train or an airplane, who insisted on smoking be charged with an offence? Who would have the responsibility of charging him or her if the law had been broken? A passenger cannot be removed from a vehicle which is airborne. There would be fairly disastrous results. It would be difficult, if not impossible, to remove a smoker from a train or a bus midway between the place of boarding and the destination.
As a non-smoker I agree with the purpose of this legislation, and I appreciate the problems many travellers experience while en route in a smoke-polluted vehicle. The question is, can a human being's habits or behaviour be totally controlled through legislation? Surely our society has not reached a level where common courtesy has disappeared and ordinary manners have been overlooked or forgotten to the extent that laws have to be enacted to force one human being to treat another in a humane manner. I would

certainly not want to believe that degree of selfishness has developed, or ever will.
I know one Canadian airline for a while placed all non-smokers toward one end of the aircraft, at the back, with smokers forward. There were too many non-smokers, so their positions had to be reversed to retain balance. This proves that the majority of the travelling public would probably welcome an arrangement whereby they could travel in a smoke-free vehicle. Would those who dislike smoke or who suffer from inhaling it be willing to have a member of their family or a friend seated elsewhere because he or she would be smoking? Would a family travelling together accept the rule, if it were in effect, that all smokers had to be seated in a separate area?
Think of the inconvenience, for example, if one parent smoked and the other did not. They would be compelled to sit in separate sections, only one of them being with the children. The father or mother would not be able to leave the smokers' area to join them because there would not be space for her or him, since the space paid for was for the entire journey.
In earlier years trains had a coach for smokers, and that did not seem to cause any problem. Passengers merely returned to the regular car until the next smoke. Theatres have designated areas for those who smoke, and many restaurants have recently set aside a room so non-smokers can enjoy their meals in comfort. One does not need to suffer from a respiratory illness to find smoke-filled air unpleasant, or even sickening, and the fact that smoke-polluted air can cause ill health, in itself should be sufficient reason for smokers to refrain from giving in to the habit while travelling, or being very sure that they are not adding, to too great an extent, to the discomfort of their fellow passengers.
With the railways and airlines in this country financially running in the red, so to speak, year after year, would they not be willing, even desirous, of formulating policies on their own to ensure the well-being, comfort and health of their customers? Perhaps a little encouragement in the right way, offering reasonable suggestions and pointing out that such a policy would be to their financial advantage, would result in positive and effective action being taken without creating force through legislation, which this bill would do.
I have been informed that at least one airline in Canada will make an attempt to take care of travellers to whom smoke is a health hazard. If the passenger cannot manage to contact officials prior to his flight time, he or she should be able to mention the fact when having his or her ticket processed. An additional simple step in the right direction would be for the stewardess who demonstrates the use of oxygen masks or serves meals, etc., to ask if anyone on the plane wishes to move to a smoke-free section, and if there is anyone who would be willing to transfer with a traveller who should be in his area because of smoking or not smoking.
If airline passengers knew the rules, and those rules were emphasized right on the ticket envelope and in ticket offices, as well as in newspaper advertisements, most adults would go along with the policy. I doubt that as
June 4, 1976

many would willingly be removed under this proposed law when smoking in a restricted section of an aircraft, be charged with breaking a law, and eventually pay the penalty, whatever it may be. Would reasonable and ordinary procedures such as this not be acceptable without adding another restriction to the lives of Canadians? Adjustment takes time, but people can be persuaded more easily than they can be forced. Good public relations must never be overlooked when one human being is associated with another.
Unfortunately there will always be those who have no feeling for or consideration of others, and there is no doubt that is why the member for Toronto-Lakeshore introduced this bill. He did so because persons have experienced difficulty, healthwise or because of concern for their future health, and I too have received representations for assistance to have a sensible policy adopted.
As far as buses are concerned, most of them are air conditioned, and little would be gained by assigning a certain number of seats for smokers. The smoke would circulate, but would be removed at the same time.
With all respect to the hon. member who sponsored this thoughtful bill, I can only repeat my earlier question: can manners be legislated? While a habit such as smoking is not ill-mannered, the abuse of any privilege is inconsiderate, and I would say that falls into the category of politeness and courtesy. To sit in a train, a bus, or a plane and blow smoke on to a fellow traveller or into the air around that person or persons is just as impolite as letting a door close behind you without looking to see if someone is following and could be hit. A program of self-analysis, through various departments is needed to point out what living is all about, that this world is made up of people, not just of one selfish, self-centred, self-indulgent human being.
Can people not place themselves in the shoes of others, at least part of the time? Could one who is a heavy smoker stop long enough to think how he or she would like fumes blown into his or her face, on to his or her clothes, and through the air around his or her immediate area? Would a smoker, whose sense of smell I have been told is not sensitive, like to breathe garlic, cheap perfume, or some unpleasant odour, for an indefinite period without any means of escape or relief?
I was amazed to realize just recently that visitors to hospitals expect to smoke right in the sickrooms. Some were indignant because they were refused entrance to an area where oxygen was in use to save lives. If that is not an example of thoughtlessness and lack of consideration, it would be hard to find one. Legislation cannot change that type of person-education and advertising could on the part of the carriers.
The solution to the problem of habitual smokers would seem to me to be one of education-signs, as used in stores; warnings in appropriate areas about health hazards to smokers and to everyone; a sentence or two added to advertisements for trips; travel agencies could co-operate. I would even go so far as to suggest that the CBC-which (jannot be interfered with by the cabinet or reached by anyone else in this Chamber who has criticism or suggestions-be instructed to remove the use of tobacco from its televised productions. Not being a TV viewer on a regular
Smoking Ban
basis, I have been told that seldom, if ever, is there a show on CBC without a cigarette or pipe hanging from the mouths of the performers.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is attempting to curb the smoking habit, and that deserves the co-operation of every Canadian. Why not have this Crown corporation, which reaches practically all homes in this country, join that department in its efforts and even mention that smoking is a health hazard? Could the CBC not have programs without anyone smoking, or consuming alcohol for that matter? If a producer feels that he is harming viewers by omitting the use of tobacco, one of the performers could say a sentence or two about polluted air, good health and how precious it is. That would be a service to smokers and non-smokers, to children and to adults, to restaurants, hotels, airlines, trains, and buses.
I understand well that it is not easy for anyone in business to try to dictate to a customer, and I would not expect that type of service. A few well placed signs, however, and the comment that there is a separate area for those who desire to smoke would not be out of place when a person enters an establishment. That would be far better than to ask people to leave after they have become settled, causing embarrassment, and more than likely losing future business.
Again I say that legislation to control the manners and personal habits of people would be looked upon as another restriction. What would the punishment be if anyone refused to avoid or leave a prohibited area on a federally controlled vehicle on land, water, or in the air? Would a traveller who broke the regulations be refused accommodation in the future? Who would decide on the penalty? How could such legislation be administered on a just basis? In my opinion the general public is already faced with and hampered by too much legislation and government interference-

Mr. Speaker, I thought I would make a few comments on this bill as well since it is connected with health in a general way. I do not think anybody will argue with the idea that non-smokers are entitled to clean air no matter where they may be, whether it be in transit or at work, at home or at play, or anywhere else.

We know from many years of experience with smoking that it is a hazardous habit creating all kinds of difficulties for many people. I suppose the most common difficulty we face is allergy. A very high percentage of Canadian people are allergic to cigarette smoke. Some of the problems it causes for them are stuffy noses, runny, itchy eyeballs, and of particular significance in transit in an aircraft is the swelling of the mucous membranes of the respiratory tract which result from the allergy which results in obstruction of the channel between the middle ear and the throat, known as the Eustachian tube. With the obstruction of this tube resulting from irritation by smoke one can experience severe middle ear pain during ascent or descent of an aircraft. For that reason alone, if for none of the many others, it is a good idea to ensure that people who have allergies to cigarette smoke are given access to transportation conveyances which are free of cigarette smoke in the interests of their own comfort.
We also know that cigarette smoke, and perhaps pipe and cigar smoke-although pipe and cigar smoke have not been incriminated as cigarette smoke has in these areas- contribute to a whole host of respiratory tract disease such as bronchitis, bronchiectasis, emphysema, and even cancer of the lung. Cancer of the lung is not necessarily the worst one because the others can lead to death as well in the long run. Most people who have studied this problem realize that cigarette smoking is a health hazard. Whether the smoke is inhaled by smoking or inhaled secondhand from someone else's exhalations, the results are the same.
However, I want to point out that over the past 30 years one particular habit has been going on; I am sure everyone has seen signs in trains, buses, airplanes and so on saying "Cigarette Smoking Only", as though cigarettes had some kind of a sweet and healthy quality about them as opposed to pipes or cigars. The fact is that in studies which have been carried out, pipe smoking and cigar smoking have been shown to be less hazardous to health than cigarette smoking. I do not want to go into the technical details of why and how, but many of the studies I have examined tend to point in that direction. Therefore it is rather strange that over the years the pipe smoker and the cigar smoker have been somewhat abused, with the cigarette smoker having his way pretty well everywhere he goes and causing a lot of trouble for the non smoking portion of the public.
What we have had for the past 30 years essentially is that pipe smokers or cigar smokers in transit have become non smokers. I think that is something we should look at very carefully. We should consider the fact that this segment of the smoking population, when in transit, does not smoke at all.

As Conservatives we believe we have faith in humanity. We believe that the ordinary citizen of this country or of any other country is a considerate and humanitarian person who is always courteous enough to consider the feelings of other people in his vicinity, and if a sign has been put up voluntarily by an airline, a bus company or a railway company, we take the position that because of this basic courtesy people tend to obey these signs regardless of whether there is a law.
On the other side of the coin, if there is someone who is so discourteous that he will not abide by a sign such as the one I have just described, then I cannot see how this law would make any difference at all. In committee we

explored in some detail the idea of the application of this bill if it should become law, and the fact is that it is almost totally impossible to enforce. The proponent of this bill himself stated that he felt there would be many occasions when it would be impossible to enforce any law emanating from this bill.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) briefly touched on the application of this law, and I would like to go into a little more detail in that regard. It seems to me that the situation is that if a smoker is in the non-smoking section of an aircraft over Saskatchewan, smoking to his heart's content and refuses to put out his cigarette when one of the beautiful hostesses asks him to do so, there is nothing more she can really do. She cannot fight or wrestle with the fellow, or hit him on the head with a club. She might simply ask him for his name, and when the aircraft lands report that name to the first policeman she can get her hands on. Normally in Canada there are RCMP constables patrolling air terminals.
I suppose the idea is that a hostess would find a policeman, point out the culprit as he was getting off the aircraft and expect the policeman to lay a charge. That looks all right on the surface, but when we consider that the laws are applied by the provinces, we have a problem. If a man is smoking over Saskatchewan and gets off the aircraft in Ontario, he cannot be charged in Ontario. He has to be charged in Saskatchewan. The RCMP would have to wire back to their colleagues in Saskatchewan to lay charges and have him appear before a magistrate there in the hope that he would plead guilty and pay the fine, or try to explain things. It is my impression that he would not feel obligated to take the next flight to Saskatchewan to face charges-indeed he might never go back at all.
We will wind up with a lot of charges on the books that will never be carried through. That just takes care of the situation within our own borders, mind you, and the international situation becomes much more complicated. If a flight lands in Canada and the offence is committed in Canada we might eventually get to the bottom of it, and perhaps the individual would be fined. If the flight is going outside Canada, to the United States, for instance, it happens that RCMP constables just do not patrol air terminals there nor in Europe. If the lady gets off the aircraft she has absolutely no recourse, nobody to whom to complain. Perhaps if she happened to come back to Canada the next day and the culprit were on the same flight she could lay a charge when she arrives in Ontario and it would be relayed to Saskatchewan. It becomes very complicated, Mr. Speaker.
There is then the problem of aliens who commit an offence over Canadian territory and refuse to abide by our laws. Once they are out of the country no charges can be laid at all. If the traveller were going outside the country the hostess would probably just forget about telling the policeman. Even if a charge were laid the chances of it being heard before a magistrate in this country are almost non-existent. So, Mr. Speaker, the proposed bill is of doubtful validity.
If an Air Canada aircraft were flying over the United States, or the ocean, or Europe, and a smoker refused to put

At last I did come across a man, John Stewart Mills, and his essay of 1859 "On Liberty". Although the flame of that essay was written 100 years ago, it burns as brightly today as the day it was lit. I want to bring to the attention of the House some quotes from that essay. I quote:
That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant. He cannot rightfully be compelled to do or forebear because it will be better for him to do so, because it will make him happier, because in the opinion of others, to do so would be wise, or even right. These are good reasons for remonstrating with him, or reasoning with him, or persuading him, or entreating him but not for compelling him, or visiting him with any evil in case he do otherwise. To justify that, the conduct from which it is desired to deter him must be calculated to produce evil to someone else. The only part of the conduct of any one, for which he is amenable to society, is that which concerns others. In the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute. Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.
I believe that this bill, in terms of the liberty of one to smoke in public places or not, has some deep implications in so far as if it would become law it would become part of our constitution, and we know that some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence and deem them like the Ark of the Covenant, too sacred to be touched. However, I know that laws and institutions must go hand and hand with the progress of the human mind.
This is the point that I want to make. The progress of the minds of Canadians is far ahead of the progress of the government and of the progress of the member opposite who is introducing this legislation. In substance, and in the spirit of this proposed legislation, I would not disagree. However, he is introducing legislation that in fact puts into place that which has already been done, accepted, and implemented by most Canadians.
